Reference: Muellbauer (1976) Basic Model To bridge the micro and macro economics, we hope that the total demand of the economy can be respresented by a so-called representative consumer, which is very difficult in practice. Traditionally, only homothetic preferences can satisfy such a requirement. However, homothetic preferences imply that the income elasticity is constant at 1, which is impossible in reality. Therefore, Muellbauer (1976) proposed Price-Independent Generalized Linear (PIGL) preference to solve such a paradox. The preference has two important two properties: (1) non-linear income elasticity (consistent with reality); (2) aggregation simplicity (easy in application). Reference : Grossman and Helpman (1991) Model Setting The paper builds a general-equilibrium model of endogenous growth in which the engine of growth is the repeated improvement of a fixed set of products. Earlier one-shot patent-race models (Loury 1979; Lee and Wilde 1980) miss the cyclical nature of quality competition: each product enjoys a limited run at the technological frontier and is then displaced. Segerstrom, Anant and Dinopoulos (1990) and Aghion and Howitt (1990) embed patent races in dynamic general equilibrium, but in the former all research is devoted to one industry at a time in sequence, and in the latter one economy-wide innovation improves all products at once. Here there is a continuum of products, each with its own quality ladder , and entrepreneurs race simultaneously in all industries to bring out the next generation of each product. Individual products climb their ladders stochastically and at different speeds, so a distribution of qualities evolves over time, but by the law of large numbers the aggregate is smooth: an index of consumption grows at a constant rate that can be computed in closed form. The main findings are four. First, the economy jumps immediately to a steady state in which the intensity of innovation rises with the size of the labour force, with the productivity of research labour and with the size of the quality step, so that R&D responds to profit incentives and the economy exhibits dynamic increasing returns to scale. Second, the market rate of innovation can be either too fast or too slow: a successful innovator creates a positive consumer-surplus and intertemporal-spillover externality and a negative business-stealing externality, and the latter dominates when the steps of the ladder are small or very large. A tax or subsidy on R&D decentralizes the optimum. Third, a model of growth through expanding product variety has exactly the same reduced form as the quality-ladder model, yet its welfare properties differ, because there equilibrium growth is always too slow. Fourth, in a two-factor, two-sector extension only a larger endowment of the factor used intensively in R&D guarantees faster growth, and in a two-country version the long-run pattern of intersectoral trade follows the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem. Producers Labour is the only primary input, and one unit of labour produces one unit of any product regardless of quality, so marginal cost equals the wage . Firms in an industry compete in prices. If several firms can make the same quality, Bertrand competition drives price to unit cost and profits to zero. If one firm has a quality lead, it charges a price that, adjusted for quality, just undercuts the unit cost of its nearest rival, and it captures the whole market. It does not charge more because it would lose all customers, and it does not charge less because industry demand is unit elastic, so revenue is independent of price while output and cost rise as price falls. In equilibrium every industry has a unique leader exactly one step ahead of its nearest rival, so all state-of-the-art products carry the same limit price and every leader earns the same profit flow: since demand per product is . A blueprint is needed to produce any quality. Patents are infinitely lived and licensing is not feasible, so only the firm that developed the state-of-the-art product manufactures it. The same outcome arises without patents if imitation is costly, since an imitator would earn zero profit in the ensuing Bertrand equilibrium. R&D Races An entrepreneur may target any product. Research at intensity for an interval of length succeeds in taking the next step up the ladder with probability and requires units of labour per unit of time. Success is therefore a Poisson process whose arrival rate depends only on current R&D activity, not on past effort. Entry into every race is free, and the input requirement is the same for incumbents and newcomers: by inspecting the goods on the market, outsiders learn enough to work on the next generation even though they cannot produce the current one. This is the public-good aspect of technology in the model. Leaders do not try to improve their own products. A leader that succeeded would be two steps ahead and could charge , so its incremental profit would be: which is strictly less than the gain of a non-leader who succeeds. Reference : Levinsohn and Petrin (2003) Model Setting The paper asks how to estimate production function parameters when input choices respond to a productivity shock that the firm observes and the econometrician does not. This simultaneity problem , raised by Marschak and Andrews (1944), makes ordinary least squares (OLS) biased: firms with a large positive shock use more inputs, so the regressors are correlated with the error. The investment proxy of Olley and Pakes (1996) controls for the shock by inverting the investment demand function, but it is only valid for plants with strictly positive investment. In plant-level data from developing countries this is restrictive, because adjustment costs make investment lumpy; in the Chilean data used here more than half of the plant-year observations report zero investment. The paper shows that an intermediate input (materials, electricity or fuels, the inputs usually subtracted out in a value-added production function) can serve as the proxy instead. Intermediate inputs are almost always positive, they are cheap to adjust and therefore respond to the whole productivity term, and, because they are not state variables, the condition that makes them a valid proxy follows from a static profit maximization problem and not from the firm's dynamic problem. The estimator has two stages. The first stage is a partially linear regression of output on the freely variable inputs and a non-parametric function of the proxy and capital, which delivers the coefficients of the variable inputs other than the proxy. The second stage uses a first-order Markov process for productivity and timing assumptions to form moment conditions that identify the coefficients on capital and on the proxy itself. Applied to the four largest Chilean manufacturing industries for 1979 to 1986, the estimator gives lower coefficients on variable inputs and higher coefficients on capital than OLS, the pattern implied by simultaneity; the estimates do not depend on whether materials or electricity is the proxy; and tests reject the equality of the intermediate input estimates with fixed effects estimates in every industry. If only labour responds to the shock and capital and labour are positively correlated, is in addition biased down. If both inputs are positively correlated with each other and labour is more strongly correlated with the shock than capital is, tends to overestimate and usually underestimates . The last two cases are the relevant ones in short panels, where identification comes mainly from between-firm variation and capital and labour are highly correlated. The standard alternatives have their own costs. The within estimator (fixed effects) protects against time-invariant firm effects but discards the between-firm variation that identifies the coefficients of state variables. Reference : Midrigan and Xu (2014) Model Setting The paper asks how much financial frictions lower aggregate total factor productivity (TFP), and through which channel. Two channels are separated. First, frictions distort entry and technology adoption , so that too few producers operate the productive technology (the extensive margin). Second, frictions create dispersion in the returns to capital across producers that already operate, which is misallocation in the sense of Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) and Hsieh and Klenow (2009) (the intensive margin). The model is an extension of the establishment dynamics model of Hopenhayn (1992) with two sectors. Producers in the unproductive traditional sector use only labor and need no finance. Producers in the productive modern sector need two kinds of capital: a one-time sunk investment to enter, and physical capital to produce. Finance is limited by simple constraints on the amount of debt and equity a producer can issue. The model is parameterized with plant-level data from Korean manufacturing (1991-1996), and its predictions are compared with plant-level data from China and Colombia, two countries with much less developed financial markets. The main finding is that financial frictions can reduce TFP, output and consumption substantially (output by up to 40 percent), but the bulk of the loss comes from the extensive margin. TFP losses from the misallocation of capital among modern-sector producers are small, at most about 5 percent in an open economy and 10 percent in a closed economy, which is one-eighth to one-fourth of the roughly 40 percent losses that Hsieh and Klenow (2009) document for China and India. The mechanism that undoes misallocation is self-financing : efficient producers accumulate internal funds and quickly grow out of their borrowing constraints, and the transitory productivity shocks measured in the data are too small to push capital far from its efficient level. Entry and adoption, in contrast, are large long-lived investments that pay off only gradually and are hard to finance from the modest profits of the traditional sector. Reference : Gibrat (1931) ; Mansfield (1962) ; Axtell (2001) Gibrat's Law, also known as the Law of Proportionate Effect, is a principle in economics and business that explains the growth dynamics of firms or cities. It was first proposed by Robert Gibrat in 1931. The law suggests that a firm's or city's growth rate is independent of its size. Key Points of Gibrat's Law (1) Proportional Growth: Gibrat's Law states that the growth rate of a firm (or city) is proportional to its current size. Formally, where is the size of the firm (or city) at time , is the growth rate, which is assumed to be random and independent of . (2) Size Independence: Growth rates are assumed to be independent of initial size. This means small firms (or cities) and large firms (or cities) have the same likelihood of experiencing similar growth rates. (3) Log-Normal Distribution: Under Gibrat's Law, the size of firms (or cities) tends to follow a log-normal distribution over time because the growth rates are multiplicative. Mathematically, the logarithm of the size ( ) will have a normal distribution if the law holds. (4) Stochastic Nature: Growth rates are often modeled as random variables with a mean and variance that do not depend on the size of the firm. Applications of Gibrat's Law (1) Firm Growth: The law has been widely used to model firm dynamics. It predicts that larger firms do not necessarily grow slower or faster than smaller firms. Example: The distribution of firm sizes in an industry may follow a log-normal or Pareto distribution as a result of Gibrat's Law. (2) Urban Economics: In city size studies, Gibrat's Law is applied to explain the growth of cities. It suggests that small and large cities grow at the same expected proportional rate, leading to the well-known Zipf's Law for city sizes. (3) Income and Wealth Distribution: Gibrat's Law has been used to explain the distribution of personal incomes or wealth under the assumption of proportionate growth in assets or earnings. Reference : Aiyagari (1994) ; Lecture Notes 1 ; Lecture Notes 2 Model Setting The paper asks how much uninsured idiosyncratic risk adds to aggregate saving. It modifies the standard growth model of Brock and Mirman (1972) by replacing the representative agent with a continuum of infinitely lived agents (of size unity) who receive idiosyncratic labor endowment shocks, cannot insure them, and can only self-insure by accumulating a single asset (capital) subject to a borrowing constraint , as in Bewley (1986). Because the shocks are purely idiosyncratic there is no aggregate uncertainty: in a steady state the interest rate, the wage, aggregate capital and the cross-section distribution of assets are constant, while each individual's assets and consumption fluctuate. Five features define the exercise: endogenous heterogeneity, aggregation, infinite horizons, a borrowing constraint, and general equilibrium (an endogenously determined interest rate). The qualitative result is that the steady-state interest rate is necessarily below the rate of time preference, so aggregate capital and the saving rate are necessarily higher than under certainty (equivalently, complete markets). The result comes from the infinite horizon and the borrowing constraint and does not require convex marginal utility, the traditional condition for precautionary saving . The quantitative result is that the effect is modest: for moderate and empirically plausible risk aversion, variability and persistence of earnings, the aggregate saving rate rises by no more than three percentage points, and only for high variability and persistence does it rise by seven to fourteen points. The model also implies that access to asset markets is valuable to individuals (consumption variability is cut by about half), and that wealth is much more dispersed than income, although less than in the data. Reference : Acemoglu et al. (2012) ; Paper Link Model Setting Can idiosyncratic shocks to individual sectors generate sizable aggregate fluctuations? The standard answer, the diversification argument of Lucas (1977), is no: in an economy of sectors hit by independent shocks, aggregate fluctuations have a magnitude proportional to , which is negligible at high levels of disaggregation. Acemoglu, Carvalho, Ozdaglar and Tahbaz-Salehi (2012) show that this argument ignores input-output linkages , which propagate a shock from a sector to its customers, to the customers of its customers, and so on. In a static multisector model in the tradition of Long and Plosser (1983), with Cobb-Douglas preferences and technologies, the log of aggregate output is a weighted sum of the log sectoral shocks, and the weights form the influence vector , which depends only on the labour share and the input-output matrix. Aggregate volatility is therefore of the order of the Euclidean norm of the influence vector, and the question becomes how fast this norm decays as the economy is disaggregated, that is, along a sequence of economies with . The paper characterizes this rate of decay in terms of structural properties of the intersectoral network . Three theorems carry the argument. A lower bound in terms of the coefficient of variation of sectoral outdegrees shows that volatility decays more slowly when a few sectors supply a disproportionate share of all inputs (first-order interconnections); with a power-law degree distribution of shape parameter , volatility is of order at least . A tighter bound adds a second-order interconnectivity coefficient, which is large when high-degree sectors share common suppliers and captures cascade effects ; with a power-law second-order degree distribution of shape parameter , volatility is of order at least . Conversely, in balanced structures, where no sector's degree grows with , volatility decays at the rate whenever the labour share is large enough, so that what matters is the asymmetry between sectors as suppliers and not the sparseness of the input-output matrix. In the US benchmark input-output tables for 1972 to 2002, both degree distributions have Pareto tails, with average estimates of 1.38 for the first-order and 1.18 for the second-order shape parameter. The latter implies that volatility decays no faster than , and a back-of-the-envelope calculation turns a sectoral standard deviation of 0.058 into an aggregate standard deviation of about 0.018, close to the roughly 2 percent standard deviation of US GDP. Reference : Baqaee and Farhi (2019) Model Setting The paper asks how a productivity shock to one producer affects aggregate output once the analysis goes beyond the first order. Hulten's theorem (Hulten 1978) states that in an efficient economy the first-order effect of a microeconomic productivity shock on aggregate output equals the producer's sales as a share of GDP, its Domar weight . The theorem implies that the production network, the elasticities of substitution, returns to scale and the scope for factor reallocation are irrelevant given observed sales, which is why Gabaix (2016) could describe networks as a particular case of granularity. The paper argues that this conclusion rests on a fragile first-order approximation. Walmart and electricity production each have sales of roughly 4 percent of US GDP, yet a large negative shock to electricity should be far more damaging. The paper derives a general second-order approximation of aggregate output for any efficient economy. Because the first derivative of log output is the Domar weight, the second derivative is the response of the Domar weight to the shock. This response is first expressed with reduced-form sufficient statistics (general equilibrium elasticities of substitution and the elasticity of the input-output multiplier) and then mapped to microeconomic primitives for nested-CES economies with arbitrary input-output linkages, and for arbitrary production functions. The main findings are as follows. Cobb-Douglas economies are a knife-edge case in which Domar weights and the whole input-output matrix are constant, the model is log-linear and Hulten's approximation is globally exact. Away from this case the second-order terms depend on microeconomic elasticities of substitution, network linkages, returns to scale and the degree of factor reallocation. With complementarities, nonlinearities amplify negative shocks and attenuate positive shocks, so that symmetric and thin-tailed sectoral shocks produce an output distribution with a lower mean, negative skewness and excess kurtosis. In a calibrated multi-sector model the mean output loss from sectoral shocks is between 0.2 and 1.3 percent, an order of magnitude above the welfare cost of business cycles of Lucas (1987). Nonlinearities almost triple the estimated effect of the 1970s oil shocks on world output, from 0.23 to 0.61 percent, and account for a reduction of about 20 percentage points in US aggregate TFP growth over 1948-2014 (Baumol's cost disease). Reference : Liu (2019) Model Setting The paper asks whether there is an economic logic to industrial policy that favours selected sectors when sectors are linked through input-output relationships and markets are imperfect. A generic formulation of market imperfections (financial frictions, contracting frictions, markups whose profits are dissipated, externalities) is embedded in a canonical nonparametric production network with constant returns. Imperfections act as wedges on intermediate input purchases, and the associated payments are quasi-rents that leave the economy as deadweight losses. A government with limited fiscal capacity cannot remove the imperfections; it can only subsidize input use in selected sectors, and the question is which sector to promote first. The central object is distortion centrality , the ratio of a sector's influence (an elasticity-based centrality) to its Domar weight (its equilibrium size). Starting from the decentralized economy without subsidies, distortion centrality is a nonparametric sufficient statistic for the social value of a marginal dollar of subsidy to a sector, and the first-order aggregate gain from any set of sectoral subsidies equals the cross-sector covariance between distortion centrality and subsidy spending per value added. Because the distortionary effects of imperfections accumulate through backward demand linkages, upstream sectors become the sink for imperfections and have the highest distortion centrality, even though they are neither the largest, the most influential, nor the most distorted sectors. In hierarchical networks this ranking is insensitive to the size and distribution of the underlying imperfections. Empirically, the input-output tables of South Korea in 1970 and China in 2007 are close to hierarchical, distortion centrality is almost perfectly correlated across many specifications of imperfections, the heavy and chemical industries promoted by South Korea in the 1970s all have distortion centrality above one, and in China sectors with high distortion centrality receive cheaper credit, more tax breaks and a larger state-owned presence. Under the preferred specification these Chinese policies together raise aggregate output by 6.7 percent to first order. Reference : Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) ; Reading Notes Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) is also an extremely influential paper in international economics. Reference : Costinot and Rodríguez-Clare (2014) ; Paper Link Model Setting This handbook chapter asks how large the welfare consequences of globalization are, and how the answer depends on the model used to compute it. It organizes the new quantitative trade literature around gravity models : general equilibrium models with constant-elasticity import demand in which bilateral trade flows satisfy a gravity equation . Two tools carry the whole analysis. The first is a sufficient-statistic welfare formula: the change in real consumption caused by a foreign shock can be inferred from the change in the share of expenditure on domestic goods and the trade elasticity . The second is the exact hat algebra popularized by Dekle, Eaton and Kortum (2008): counterfactual changes in trade flows and incomes solve a nonlinear system that involves only observed trade shares, incomes and the trade elasticity, so that preference shifters, endowments and trade costs never need to be estimated. Starting from the Armington model, the chapter adds, one at a time, alternative market structures (perfect competition, monopolistic competition with free entry, firm heterogeneity as in Melitz with Pareto productivity), multiple sectors, tradable intermediate goods and multiple factors, and for each variant it derives the gravity equation and the formula for the gains from trade , defined as the absolute value of the percentage change in real income from moving to autarky. All models are calibrated to the same data, the World Input-Output Database (WIOD) for 2008 with 27 EU countries and 13 other major countries, and to the same trade elasticities, so differences in predictions come from different counterfactual equilibria and not from different fits of the initial equilibrium. The headline numbers are as follows. In the one-sector model the gains from trade average 4.4 percent and are 1.8 percent for the United States. Multiple sectors with Cobb-Douglas upper-level preferences raise the average to about 15 percent, tradable intermediate goods to about 27 percent, and monopolistic competition with intermediates to 32 percent (Krugman) and 40 percent (Melitz). For trade policy, the optimal unilateral tariff in the Armington model is close to 20 percent and its gains are small (0.3 percent for the United States), while a worldwide 40 percent tariff lowers real consumption by 2.3 percent on average in the one-sector model and by 7.0 percent in a model with intermediates and firm heterogeneity. Reference : Caliendo and Parro (2015) Model Setting The paper builds sectoral linkages , trade in intermediate goods and sectoral heterogeneity in production into the Ricardian model of Eaton and Kortum (2002) in order to quantify the trade and welfare effects of tariff changes, and applies it to the tariff reductions of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) between Mexico, Canada and the U.S. The motivation is that sectors and countries are interrelated. A tariff cut in one sector lowers prices in that sector, in the sectors that buy materials from it, and in non-tradable sectors that use tradable inputs, and non-tradables are most of final demand (more than 80 percent in the U.S. in 1993). Three facts make this important for NAFTA. Tariffs were heterogeneous across sectors: in 1993 the average sectoral tariffs applied to NAFTA partners were 12.5 percent (Mexico), 4.2 percent (Canada) and 2.7 percent (U.S.). Most trade is in intermediate goods: 82.1, 72.3 and 72.8 percent of the imports of Mexico, Canada and the U.S. from NAFTA partners. And input-output (I-O) tables show that sectors buy most inputs from other sectors (the mean own-sector share is 16 percent in the U.S. and 13 percent in Mexico), with tradables supplying 23 to 32 percent of the inputs of non-tradables and non-tradables 26 to 34 percent of the inputs of tradables. The paper makes three contributions. First, a tractable multi-country, multi-sector model with tradable and non-tradable sectors linked through an I-O structure, which is solved in relative changes (the hat algebra of Dekle, Eaton and Kortum 2008) and reduces to one equation per country; the only parameters to estimate are the sectoral trade elasticities . Second, a new estimator of these elasticities that uses a triple ratio of bilateral trade flows and tariffs, needs no symmetry of trade costs and no data on domestic sales, and is valid in any model with a multiplicative gravity equation. Third, a quantification with 31 countries and 40 sectors calibrated to 1993. NAFTA's tariff reductions raise welfare by 1.31 percent in Mexico and 0.08 percent in the U.S. and lower it by 0.06 percent in Canada; intra-bloc trade rises by 118 percent for Mexico, 11 percent for Canada and 41 percent for the U.S. Welfare and trade effects are much smaller in models without sectoral heterogeneity, intermediate goods or I-O linkages. Reference : Antràs, Redding and Rossi-Hansberg (2023) Model Setting The paper asks how globalization shapes the emergence and severity of pandemics , and how a pandemic in turn feeds back on trade. It combines two mechanisms. First, international trade requires travel: households must meet sellers face to face to source their varieties, so trade and travel both follow a constant elasticity gravity equation that depends on trade and mobility frictions. Second, travel produces human interactions that transmit disease as in a multi-country susceptible-infected-recovered ( SIR ) model. The difference from existing multigroup SIR models is that the matrix of contacts between countries is an equilibrium outcome of the trade model, so trade costs and travel restrictions determine whether a pandemic occurs and how large it is. There are four sets of results. (i) Trade-motivated travel creates an epidemiological externality : a global pandemic occurs whenever any single country has a reproduction number based on its domestic interactions above one, so a country that has the disease under control at home cannot escape a pandemic if its trade partners do not. (ii) Lower trade or travel frictions have an ambiguous effect on the global reproduction number, because they raise the total number of interactions and also make households substitute foreign for domestic interactions; with symmetric countries integration makes pandemics more likely and more severe, and with sufficiently different disease environments it can do the opposite. (iii) If the disease kills or lowers the labor supply of the infected, the relative wage of the unhealthy country rises and travel to it falls, a general equilibrium social distancing effect that operates without any individual awareness. (iv) If agents internalize the risk of infection, they cut interactions, and cut foreign interactions by more, so that the ratio of trade to GDP falls sharply early in the pandemic and recovers afterwards. The baseline model has two countries, one sector and no behavioral response; all proofs, the parameter values behind the figures and a long list of extensions (remote trade, a dynamic version in which travel is needed only to start a relationship, many countries and sectors, intermediate inputs, scale economies, imperfect competition) are in the online appendix. Motivating Evidence The paper first documents that disease spreads faster to places with stronger trade links, using three diseases: the medieval plague (European cities, 1347 to 1760, first arrival in Messina), the 1957-1958 influenza and COVID-19 (countries, first outbreak in China). The outcome is the log of the arrival time, the time between the first outbreak anywhere and the first outbreak in a location; trade is measured before each outbreak, and all variables are standardized so that coefficients are beta coefficients (robust standard errors in parentheses). Plague : across 1,149 cities, log trade access (the inverse of the distance to the nearest Old World trade route) has a coefficient of (0.0348), controlling for log distance from Messina, 0.108 (0.0302). Influenza 1957-1958 : across 52 countries, log trade with China in 1956 has a coefficient of (0.1048), with log distance at 0.560 (0.0867). COVID-19 : across 172 countries, log trade with China in 2019 has a coefficient of (0.0742), with log distance at 0.301 (0.0819). Adding the log migrant stock gives (0.0804) for trade and (0.0920) for migrants. Adding the log of total arrivals and departures of people between each country and China gives 0.0195 (0.1012) for trade, (0.0945) for migrants and (0.1259) for arrivals and departures: trade stops mattering once movements of people are held fixed, as expected if travel is the mechanism. Travel and trade : in a panel of origin-destination-year observations from 1982 to 2019 with pair and year fixed effects (124,597 observations), a 1 percent increase in bilateral trade is associated with a 0.217 percent (0.0111) increase in bilateral air passengers. The elasticity is 0.293 (0.0173) for pairs more than 3,000 kilometers apart and 0.230 (0.0134) when trade is restricted to goods for which air transport is below 20 percent of trade value. Instrumenting trade with bilateral tariffs gives 0.399 (0.1574) with a first-stage F-statistic of 100.8, and the reduced-form coefficient of log air passengers on the log tariff is (0.3682). The authors do not claim that these estimates are causal, because in the model trade and travel are jointly determined by the same frictions; they point to quasi-experimental studies (Soderlund 2020; Campante and Yanagizawa-Drott 2018) for causal evidence. Reference : Arkolakis, Eckert and Shi (2023) Model Setting A combinatorial discrete choice problem (CDCP) is the problem of choosing the combination of items that maximizes an objective function when the value of each item depends on which other items are also chosen. A multinational firm selecting production locations is the leading example: plants in Germany and the United States may create scale economies that raise the value of both, while plants in Germany and France may cannibalize each other in the European market. Without structure on the objective function the problem is NP-hard and the decision maker must evaluate all combinations, which is more than one million with only twenty items. The paper develops an exact solution method that applies whenever the objective satisfies a single crossing differences condition, a condition weaker than requiring items to be complements (supermodularity) or substitutes (submodularity). The method discards suboptimal combinations without computing their payoffs, always recovers the global optimum, and extends to heterogeneous agents, for whom it delivers the exact policy function mapping each type to its optimal combination. It builds on Jia (2008), whose method covers only the complements case and falls back on brute force over whatever part of the domain is left; the paper extends the elimination logic to substitutes, replaces the brute-force step with a branching procedure, and avoids discretizing agent heterogeneity. The application is a general equilibrium model of multinational production (MP) in which heterogeneous firms choose sets of production locations subject to fixed costs. An additional plant raises firm-level scale economies but cannibalizes the firm's other plants, and a single ratio of two elasticities determines which force wins. The model is calibrated to trade, affiliate sales and affiliate counts for 32 OECD and European countries, for 37 different degrees of complementarity or substitutability. The method is up to four to five orders of magnitude faster than brute force and one to two orders of magnitude faster than the Jia (2008) approach on a productivity grid, and it removes a discretization error in aggregate flows that exceeds 20 percent even on a grid of 16,384 points. Quantitatively, the stronger the complementarity among locations, the more the welfare gains from MP concentrate in the headquarter countries of the most productive firms, and some countries that mainly host foreign affiliates lose; with substitutability, gains are positive and more even. Reference : Castro-Vincenzi (2024) Model Setting The paper asks how the likelihood of extreme weather events shapes the spatial organization of firms , and how much firm-level adaptation can buffer the cost of climate change. The setting is the global car industry: multinational, multiplant firms that produce tradable goods in physical sites exposed to floods. Two adaptation margins are studied. Ex ante, firms choose where to locate plants and how much capacity to install in each. Ex post, multiplant firms reallocate production from disrupted to undisrupted plants, up to the capacity installed there. An event study on plant-level data for 2000 to 2019 shows that a severe flood near an assembly plant lowers its output persistently and that sibling plants of the same firm raise theirs. The paper then builds a static, quantitative, multiregion model in which a firm makes sunk capacity investments in many locations before local productivity shocks are realized, and afterwards chooses production flows from each plant to each market subject to the capacity constraints. The firm trades off proximity to large markets, low production and capacity costs, and resilience : because a plant can be an export platform for any market, holding capacity in several locations, and more capacity than is used in normal times, is a hedge against disruption of one plant. The methodological contribution is that plant location is not treated as a combinatorial discrete choice with fixed costs. Capacity is continuous with a strictly positive marginal cost at zero, so a location is left empty when the expected shadow value of its first unit of capacity is below that cost. The resulting ex ante problem is a convex optimization problem , whose dual can be written as a conic program that standard solvers handle very quickly. The model is estimated on the 2019 geography of car production and combined with CMIP6 projections of extreme precipitation for 2035 to 2064. Under the high-emissions scenario SSP5-8.5, firms build more but smaller plants and hold more spare capacity, firm size and profits fall by 4 to 5 percent, and adaptation averts about one fifth of the profit loss. Consumers, however, are worse off with adaptation than without it, because the reorganization of production lowers the productivity and capacity of every variety at once. Reference : Allen and Donaldson (2022) Model Setting The paper asks how much of today's spatial distribution of economic activity is determined by history and not by geographic fundamentals, how long a temporary local shock should be expected to affect local economic concentration, and when such a shock has permanent consequences. It builds a deliberately simple dynamic model of economic geography with an arbitrary number of heterogeneous locations that interact through migration, with agglomeration externalities in production and in amenities and with endogenous fertility. The model is a primer on Allen and Donaldson (2020). When locations interact through trade and migration, the equilibrium is a system of equations with a block structure, one block for each source of interaction across locations, and the earlier paper has four blocks. Two simplifications reduce the system to one block in the vector of local populations. First, there are no trade costs and all locations produce one homogeneous good, which removes the block that determines nominal wages from exports and the block that determines the cost of living from imports. Second, parents have more children when those children expect high lifetime welfare, and under one parameter restriction this force exactly offsets the usual tendency of attractive origins to send out fewer migrants, which merges the two migration blocks (attractiveness as a destination and as a birthplace) into one. Three terms organize the analysis. Multiplicity means that the transition from one period to the next is indeterminate. Persistence is the slow decay of the effect of a temporary change in historical conditions when the equilibrium is unique. Path dependence means that a temporary change has permanent effects because it moves the economy towards a different steady state. The central message is the distinction between spillovers that affect productivity or amenities contemporaneously and spillovers that act with a lag of one generation. There are four results. The dynamic equilibrium is unique and stable when total contemporaneous spillovers are weaker than the dispersion force. Local persistence in partial equilibrium is higher when either contemporaneous or historical spillovers are large. Persistence of the whole economy in general equilibrium is governed by the sum of contemporaneous and historical spillovers. 的入门版本。当地区之间通过贸易和移民相互作用时，均衡是一个具有分块结构的方程组，每一种跨地区的相互作用对应一个方程块，而此前那篇论文有四个方程块。两项简化把方程组降为关于各地人口向量的一个方程块。第一，不存在贸易成本，所有地区生产同一种同质产品，这就去掉了由出口决定名义工资的方程块和由进口决定生活成本的方程块。第二，当子女预期的终身福利较高时，父母会生育更多子女；在一个参数约束下，这一力量恰好抵消了有吸引力的出生地向外输送较少移民的通常倾向，从而把两个移民方程块（作为目的地的吸引力和作为出生地的吸引力）合并为一个。 Reference : Faber and Gaubert (2019) Model Setting The paper studies the long-run economic consequences of tourism , a fast-growing services export of developing countries, both locally and in the aggregate. The conventional view holds that agglomeration economies reside in manufacturing, so that a reallocation of factors into services could act as a form of Dutch disease. The setting is Mexico, where tourism emerged in the 1950s and 1960s and now accounts for about 10 percent of GDP; the 150 coastal municipalities (14 percent of the population) receive 63.5 percent of national hotel revenues, and roughly 80 percent of tourism revenue comes from domestic visitors and 20 percent from foreigners. The paper proceeds in two parts. The first estimates the local effects of tourism in the cross-section of 2,455 municipalities, using geological, oceanographic and archaeological variation in ex ante tourism attractiveness along the coastline as instruments for local hotel revenues. The second builds a quantitative spatial equilibrium model in the spirit of Allen and Arkolakis (2014), Ahlfeldt et al. (2015) and Redding (2016), with trade in goods, trade in tourism services through travelling consumers, labour mobility, input-output linkages, tax-financed public investment in tourism, and within-sector and cross-sector agglomeration spillovers on manufacturing. Because cross-sectional regressions identify only relative effects, the model is needed to recover the aggregate implications that are consistent with the estimated local effects. The main findings are as follows. A 10 percent increase in local hotel revenues raises municipality employment by 2.5 percent and nominal GDP by 4 percent, in part through a multiplier effect on manufacturing GDP of 3.9 percent. Through the lens of the model, about 60 percent of the local GDP effect comes from neoclassical forces and the rest from agglomeration forces, with an estimated within-manufacturing spillover elasticity of 0.064 and a cross-sector spillover elasticity of 0.087 from services to manufacturing. Tourism raises the welfare of the average Mexican household by 4.64 percent net of the cost of public investment, of which about 40 percent (1.82 percent) is due to international tourism. Spillovers contribute only about one-tenth of the aggregate gain (the gain would be 4.25 percent without them): they generate large reallocations towards touristic regions, but the local gains are largely offset by lower agglomeration economies in less touristic regions, so the national gains mainly reflect a classical market integration effect. The coefficient of this regression is distinct from the tourism parameter of the model below. Standard errors are clustered by municipality. Three measures of attractiveness are used: (i) a dummy for an offshore island within 5 km of the coastline; (ii) the fraction of pixels within 100 m of the shoreline covered by white sand beach , classified from 1987-1997 LandSat images at 30 m resolution as falling within the wavelength ranges of the eight top-ranked Mexican beaches; and (iii) a dummy for pre-Hispanic archaeological ruins . Since the island and beach measures are zero inland and the fixed effects are coast-by-period, the identifying variation is within coastal municipalities. Because tourism was negligible before 1960, the cross-section captures the long-run effect of tourism exposure. In the reduced form, a one standard deviation increase in a standardized attractiveness score raises employment by 33 percent, population by 24 percent, the wage bill by about 80 percent, GDP by 74 percent, manufacturing GDP by about 45 percent (coefficient 0.451) and Mincerized wages by 7.6 percent. Placebo regressions on census populations of 1921-1950 give small, negative and insignificant coefficients; model-based residential amenities are not significantly correlated with the instruments; and a panel design that interacts attractiveness with national tourist arrivals (instrumented with US air fares) confirms the results. The IV specification replaces attractiveness by log hotel sales (inverse hyperbolic sine), instrumented with the three measures jointly (first-stage F-statistic 15.13). The IV coefficients, with standard errors in parentheses, are 0.245 (0.041) for employment, 0.200 (0.042) for population, 0.475 (0.069) for labour income, 0.404 (0.071) for GDP, 0.394 (0.094) for manufacturing GDP, 0.102 (0.150) for agricultural GDP and 0.0446 (0.0057) for the wage residual. Reference : Loumeau (2024) Model Setting The paper asks whether New Towns , planned large urban sub-centres, are a good way to accommodate rising urbanisation. Since 1900, 785 metropolitan areas have developed New Towns, with an average target population of 264,436 residents. Their rationale is the co-location hypothesis : decentralising jobs and housing into sub-centres improves the spatial match between residence and workplace and shortens commutes. Reduced-form studies cannot separate this pure urban-structure effect from other equilibrium responses, in particular from induced population growth. The paper builds a quantitative spatial general equilibrium model in the spirit of Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf (2015), designed for large-scale urban master plans . A master plan has three components: location-specific availability of residential and commercial land, investments in the metropolitan transport network, and a head tax that finances both. Heterogeneous workers choose a residence-workplace pair, firms of different sectors compete for commercial floor space, and, as in Heblich, Redding and Sturm (2020), the metropolitan area is an open city embedded in a national economy, so that its population responds to welfare inside the area relative to a reservation utility outside. The application is the five New Towns of the Paris metropolitan area (Cergy-Pontoise, Evry, Marne-la-Vallee, Melun-Senart and St-Quentin-en-Yvelines, 70 municipalities in total), built from 1969 under the 1965 master plan and connected to the historical centre by the rapid suburban rail network (RER lines A to D). The government secured 44,862 hectares of building land, of which 24,086 hectares were bought at an average of 13.04 francs per square metre, and 184,238 housing units were built in the New Towns between 1969 and 1990. The calibrated model compares the observed plan with three alternative plans that distribute the same total amount of new land differently. By 2015, relative to a plan that scales up the 1968 land distribution, New Towns raise metropolitan population by 18.46 percent (868,628 residents), raise metropolitan GDP by 11.4 percent (3.27 billion euros) and lower average commuting time by 6.9 percent (0.86 minutes). Because the population effect dominates, total commuting time rises by 10.29 percent. The 2015 census counts slightly more than 800,000 residents in the New Towns, fewer than the induced population, so the New Towns “generated” their own occupants and did not accommodate pre-existing urban growth, a land-use counterpart of the fundamental law of highway congestion. Without the accompanying transport investments the New Town plan is dominated by the scaled-up plan. A difference-in-differences analysis of 314 New Towns opened worldwide between 1992 and 2012 gives a GDP effect of about 10.5 percent, close to the structural estimate for Paris. The national economy has an exogenous mass of workers , of which the endogenous mass lives in the metropolitan area; there is no commuting across its border. An urban master plan specifies the residential land available in location and the commercial land available in location , both weakly increasing over time, so that in each period the planner only decides where to place the newly available land. Reference : Tsivanidis (2026) Model Setting The paper asks how large the economic gains from urban public transit are once people can change where they live and work, firms can relocate, and wages and floorspace prices adjust. The setting is TransMilenio in Bogota, the world's most-used bus rapid transit (BRT) system: opened in 2000 and extended in 2006 and 2012, it has 147 stations and more than 2.2 million daily riders, with dedicated lanes, operating speeds of about 26 km per hour (against roughly 10 km per hour on the incumbent buses), and feeder buses to terminals at no extra fare. Before the system, 73 percent of commuters used buses, car commutes were about 36 percent faster than bus commutes, and low-educated residents were about 23 percent more likely to use buses, so the distributional effects are also of interest. The standard evaluation tool is the value of travel time savings (VTTS), which misses reallocation and general equilibrium effects. The paper builds a quantitative urban model with two skill groups, car ownership, several commute modes, nonhomothetic (Stone-Geary) housing demand, multiple industries, and productivity and amenity externalities. A special case with one group yields a log-linear reduced form in which the transit network matters only through commuter market access (CMA): resident CMA (access to jobs) and firm CMA (access to workers). The elasticities of population, employment and floorspace prices to CMA, together with the change in CMA, are sufficient statistics for the effects of transit in a broad class of models. These elasticities are estimated on 2,799 census tracts with data from before and after construction. The main findings are that the VTTS captures only 52 percent of the general equilibrium welfare gain (1.25 against 2.39 percent); that welfare rose by 2.34 percent and GDP by 3.25 percent in a closed city (0.69 and 17.5 percent with migration); that the high-skilled gain slightly more, so welfare inequality rises by a modest 0.59 percent; and that a well-targeted zoning reform would have raised the welfare gain by about 36 percent. Reference : Berry (1992) Model Setting The paper studies entry into airline city-pair markets. The central idea is to use observed entry decisions to infer underlying firm profitability while allowing for two features that are essential in oligopoly markets: (1) firms are heterogeneous in their profitability; (2) profitability depends on the number of competing firms that enter. Consider market with potential entrants. Firm chooses whether to enter the market, Let denote the number of firms that enter. The post-entry profit of firm is specified as where is the component of profits common to firms in market and captures firm-specific profitability. The key assumption is Thus, additional entry reduces the profitability of all firms. This captures competitive pressure without specifying a complete pricing or quantity-setting game. The firm-specific term allows different airlines to have different profitability in the same city-pair market. In the airline application, an important source of such heterogeneity is the airline's existing presence at the two endpoint airports. Entry Equilibrium A pure-strategy Nash equilibrium requires that every entering firm earns nonnegative profits and every non-entering firm would earn negative profits if it entered. Because firms differ in , order them from most to least profitable: The equilibrium number of firms is The intuition is straightforward. If the th most profitable firm can earn positive profits when there are firms in the market, then the market can support at least firms. Conversely, if the th most profitable firm cannot earn positive profits when there are firms, the market cannot support firms. Uniqueness of the Number of Firms An important result is that the identities of entering firms need not be unique, but the equilibrium number of firms is unique. Suppose is defined by and Consider an alternative equilibrium with more than firms. The least profitable entering firm must have profitability no greater than . It therefore could not earn positive profits, contradicting the equilibrium condition. A similar contradiction rules out an equilibrium with fewer than firms. Hence, even though different sets of firms may enter. This result is important empirically because the econometrician can use the equilibrium number of firms without having to resolve equilibrium multiplicity over firm identities. Firm-specific profitability is where contains observed firm characteristics and represents unobserved firm heterogeneity. Observed and Unobserved Firm Heterogeneity The model distinguishes two forms of firm heterogeneity. Observed heterogeneity is contained in while unobserved heterogeneity is contained in In the airline application, the main observed firm-specific variables measure airport presence. Let be an indicator equal to one if airline already operates at both endpoint cities of market . Let measure the airline's average share of airport output at the two endpoint cities. The more serious problem is the complicated region of the unobservables associated with a given equilibrium outcome. For example, determining the probability that exactly firms are profitable requires considering all possible subsets of firms among potential entrants. The number of such subsets is In the airline data, the number of potential entrants can be as large as 26. For example, Thus, likelihood evaluation may require millions of separate regions of integration, and these calculations must be repeated many times during numerical optimization. Firms are heterogeneous, but one firm's entry has no effect on another firm's profitability. Alternatively, if there is no unobserved firm heterogeneity, firms can be ranked entirely using observed characteristics. The second channel allows transmission expansion to change the profitability of renewable investment and therefore the long-run generation capacity. The key empirical point is that renewable investment may occur in anticipation of future market integration, so a standard before-and-after comparison may fail to capture the full effect. First, the observed reduction in generation costs around the transmission opening tends to understate the full long-run cost reduction: Second, the observed reduction in electricity prices tends to understate the full price effect because solar entry has already depressed pre-integration prices. A project first chooses a balancing authority (market) and then chooses a county within the selected market. Developers choose locations to maximize project profitability, which depends on expected revenues, installation costs, local characteristics, and place-based tax credits. For project locating in county within market , static operating profit in period is: where is the electricity price, is annual electricity generation, and denotes operation and maintenance costs. The net present value of the project is: where denotes location-specific installation costs. Annual generation is approximated by project nameplate capacity multiplied by the technology-specific capacity factor. Electricity prices are approximated using annual county-level average prices. County Choice The baseline specification assumes that projects take the Production Tax Credit (PTC). Let denote the baseline PTC rate and the Energy Community bonus. The utility from locating project in county is: where indicates whether county is eligible for the Energy Community tax credit. The vector includes local characteristics such as average farm size, average farm value, and distance to transmission infrastructure. The error term follows a Type-I Extreme Value distribution. Installation costs are not directly observed and are constructed from technology-specific levelized costs: where is the local capacity factor, denotes fixed operation and maintenance costs, and is project capacity. Developers are allowed to differ in their sensitivity to revenues and capital costs. The random coefficients are specified as: where indicates whether the project is paired with battery storage and is drawn from a standard normal distribution. Conditional on project-specific coefficients, the probability that project chooses county within market takes the standard logit form: where denotes the deterministic component of county-level utility. Market Choice County-level profitability is aggregated into a project-market-specific inclusive value: A market containing more profitable county-level alternatives therefore has a higher inclusive value. Project chooses market according to: where includes market-level characteristics such as Renewable Portfolio Standard targets, residential and industrial electricity consumption, and an indicator for whether the balancing authority operates a wholesale electricity market. captures region-specific factors, and follows a Type-I Extreme Value distribution. The sensitivity to within-market profitability is heterogeneous across projects: where is drawn from a standard normal distribution. Estimation The model is estimated separately for wind and solar projects using a sequential random-coefficients logit procedure. First, the authors estimate the county-level choice model. Because some balancing authorities contain hundreds of counties, the full county choice set is computationally costly. For each project, the authors therefore construct a sampled choice set containing the observed chosen county and approximately 25 alternative counties. Alternatives are sampled with higher probabilities when they are similar to the chosen county in renewable capacity factors, levelized costs, agricultural characteristics, terrain, zoning restrictions, and transmission infrastructure. To correct for the non-random sampling of alternatives, the log county inclusion probability enters the likelihood as an offset with its coefficient constrained to one. Second, the estimated county-level parameters are used to calculate the deterministic utility for each project-county pair and construct the inclusive value: Third, the market-level random-coefficients logit is estimated using together with observed market characteristics: Finally, because the inclusive value used in the market-choice model is a generated regressor from the county-choice estimation, standard errors are obtained using a bootstrap procedure that jointly resamples projects and markets. This propagates first-stage estimation uncertainty through the construction of inclusive values and into the market-level parameter estimates. Counterfactuals and Welfare The estimated model is used to evaluate alternative Energy Community tax-credit designs. A change in eligibility or the subsidy rate changes county-level profitability, which affects county choice probabilities, inclusive values, and ultimately market choice probabilities. Producer surplus is calculated using the log-sum expression: where converts utility changes into dollar values. Expected renewable capacity in a set of targeted counties is obtained from predicted location probabilities: The counterfactual exercises hold the number and size of projects fixed. Therefore, policy changes affect the spatial allocation of renewable capacity rather than endogenous project entry or total renewable investment. Time is discrete and indexed by year . A wind farm first decides whether to enter the market or wait. The model therefore consists of three components: bilateral bargaining between wind farms and utilities, buyer choice and non-utility demand, and dynamic entry under policy uncertainty. The first two components determine the expected profit from entering in year , while the dynamic problem determines the optimal timing of entry. Reference : Gerarden (2023) Model Setting The model follows the dynamic oligopoly framework of Ericson and Pakes (1995) . There are incumbent solar panel manufacturers competing in regional markets over discrete time periods. Firms produce an undifferentiated product and compete in quantities in each regional market. Firms share a common discount factor . Firm is characterized by its energy conversion efficiency, , which determines its production cost. The industry state is where is the distribution of firms' energy conversion efficiencies, is a common input price, and is the vector of market-specific demand states. Within each period, firms first observe the industry state and private investment shocks. They then compete in the product market and choose whether to invest in improving energy conversion efficiency. Investment outcomes are realized at the beginning of the next period. Demand and Product Market Competition Demand in market is static and given by where is total solar panel demand, is the market price, and is the consumer subsidy. Subsidies shift the demand state . Firms compete à la Cournot. Firm chooses quantity in market to maximize static product-market profits: The resulting equilibrium product-market profit of firm is denoted by Marginal costs depend on the firm's energy conversion efficiency and the common input price. Higher energy conversion efficiency reduces the amount of material required to produce a given amount of electricity-generating capacity and therefore lowers production costs. Dynamic Investment Firms make a binary investment decision, where denotes an investment in R&D and physical capital that improves future energy conversion efficiency. Firm 's per-period payoff is where is the fixed cost of investment and is an i.i.d. Type-I extreme value private shock. Energy conversion efficiency evolves according to where is a stochastic efficiency improvement conditional on investment. Thus, investment lowers future marginal costs by improving the firm's technology. The firm's value function is Consumer subsidies affect innovation by increasing demand and therefore increasing the future profit gain from lowering marginal costs. Equilibrium Firms follow Markov strategies that depend only on the current industry state and their private shocks. A Markov-perfect Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile such that, for every firm , for every state, private shock, and alternative strategy . Estimation: Demand and Production Costs The model is estimated in two broad steps. First, the product-market model, state transitions, and firms' investment policy functions are estimated. Second, these estimates are used to recover the structural cost of investment. Demand is assumed to be log-linear: where is the price elasticity of demand and captures the effect of consumer subsidies. Price is instrumented using input prices and, in the baseline specification, solar panel prices in other geographic markets. The estimated demand parameters are used with firms' Cournot first-order conditions to recover marginal costs. Under constant-elasticity demand, The relationship between production costs and observed energy conversion efficiency is estimated using where denotes observed energy conversion efficiency. The parameter maps improvements in observed efficiency into reductions in marginal costs. Estimation: State Transitions and Investment Policy The exogenous states, including the common input price and market-specific demand states, are assumed to follow first-order Markov processes: Because an improvement in a firm's energy conversion efficiency is assumed to occur if and only if the firm invests, observed efficiency changes reveal the binary investment decision . The conditional probability of investment is approximated parametrically. The author first uses LASSO to select variables from a flexible function of the firm's own efficiency and the industry state, and then estimates a logit model using the selected covariates: Conditional on investment, the size of the efficiency improvement, , is estimated using a Gamma distribution. Estimation: Dynamic Investment Costs The fixed cost of innovation, , is estimated using a two-step forward-simulation estimator following Bajari, Benkard and Levin (2007) . The ex-ante value function can be written as Because flow payoffs are linear in the structural parameters, the value function can be expressed as where contains the fixed investment cost and the scale of the private investment shocks. The function is approximated by forward simulation. Starting from each observed state, future investment decisions are simulated using the estimated investment policy function, efficiency improvements are drawn from their estimated distribution, and future demand and input prices evolve according to the estimated state transition processes. These simulations generate expected discounted product-market profits and investment decisions. The structural parameter is then estimated by pseudo maximum likelihood using the firm's optimal investment decision. Intuitively, is identified by comparing the model-implied future profit gains from investment across industry states with the observed frequency of investment in those states. A state in which investment generates large future profits but firms invest infrequently implies a relatively high fixed cost of innovation. Reference : Johnston (2019) Model Setting The model studies a wind developer's choice between two subsidy schemes: the Production Tax Credit (PTC) and the Section 1603 cash grant. Project characteristics are taken as given when the subsidy choice is made. Let denote the installation cost of project and denote its expected annual electricity generation. The key structural parameter is , which measures the developer's valuation of one dollar of nonrefundable tax benefits relative to one dollar of cash. A value of implies that tax credits and cash are valued equally, while captures the loss in value associated with the nonrefundability of tax credits. If project chooses the PTC, it receives a per-MWh tax credit for the first ten years of operation. The expected present value of the PTC is where is the real discount factor. Assuming expected annual generation is constant over time, , this can be written as where is determined by the discount factor and the PTC schedule. If the project chooses the grant, it receives 30% of installation cost. However, choosing the grant reduces the depreciable tax basis by 15% of installation cost. The present value of the grant is therefore where captures the present value of depreciation deductions, given the tax rate and discount factor. The developer chooses the subsidy with the higher expected value: Thus, more productive projects are more likely to choose the PTC, while higher-cost projects are more likely to choose the grant. Estimation Let be an indicator equal to one if project chooses the grant. To allow for unobserved determinants of subsidy choice, the model introduces an additive error term. Since the variance of these unobservables is assumed to increase with project size, the subsidy values are normalized by nameplate capacity. Let The subsidy choice equation becomes A key empirical problem is that installation cost is observed only for projects that choose the grant, because the grant amount equals 30% of eligible installation cost. The author therefore specifies a cost equation where contains observed determinants of construction cost, including project size, turbine characteristics, construction wages, developer experience, region, and time controls. The unobserved cost shock and the unobserved subsidy-choice shock are assumed to follow a bivariate standard normal distribution: where captures the correlation between unobserved construction costs and unobserved preferences for the grant. Maximum Likelihood Estimation The cost equation and the subsidy-choice equation are jointly estimated by maximum likelihood. For projects that choose the grant, both the subsidy choice and installation cost are observed. Their likelihood contribution can be written schematically as For projects that choose the PTC, installation cost is unobserved. The likelihood therefore integrates over all possible values of the latent installation cost: Under the joint normality assumption, this integral can be expressed using the normal CDF. The parameters are estimated jointly by maximizing the likelihood over all projects. Identification The valuation parameter is identified from how projects trade off installation cost against expected electricity generation when choosing between the two subsidies. Higher increases the value of the PTC, whereas higher increases the value of the grant. The observed switching pattern between the two subsidies therefore identifies the relative valuation of tax credits and cash. To identify the selection model, expected generation per unit of capacity, , is excluded from the cost equation. It directly affects the subsidy choice through the value of the PTC but is assumed not to directly affect construction cost conditional on : Thus, shifts the probability of selecting the grant without directly shifting the conditional mean of installation cost. The valuation parameter is difficult to separately identify from the discount factor . The paper therefore calibrates using a 7% real discount rate rather than jointly estimating it with . The estimate implies that wind developers value one dollar of nonrefundable tax credits at approximately $0.85 relative to one dollar of cash grant. Reference : Shapiro (2025) Model Setting The paper proposes that strong institutions give a country comparative advantage in clean industries and thereby improve its environmental quality. This supply-side channel is set beside three established explanations of the global distribution of pollution: weak environmental regulation (the Pollution Havens Hypothesis), capital endowments that attract capital-intensive dirty industries (Heckscher-Ohlin), and income (the Environmental Kuznets Curve). Three institutions are studied: financial, judicial and labour market institutions. Five complementary tests are used. First, industries that depend on institutions are clean. Second, strong institutions raise relative exports of clean industries. Third, the complexity of an industry helps explain the link. Fourth, cross-country differences in the composition of output account for an important share of cross-country differences in emissions. Fifth, a quantitative general equilibrium trade model shows that strengthening a country's institutions lowers its own pollution by relocating dirty industries abroad, and raises pollution in other countries. Cost structure explains why institutions, which do not target pollution, can matter as much as environmental regulation: regulation raises the costs of the dirtiest industries by at most a few percent, whereas institutions change the productivity of intermediate goods and factors, which make up most of a firm's costs. Country institutions are measured around 2012 in z-scores, with higher values denoting better institutions. Financial institutions are private credit by deposit money institutions relative to GDP, judicial institutions are the World Bank Rule of Law index, and labour market institutions are the Heritage Foundation labour market freedom index (flexibility of hiring, firing and hours). The institutions index is their first principal component. Environmental regulation is the first principal component of four of eight available measures (diesel sulphur standard, survey measures of stringency and of enforcement, number of environmental treaties). Factor endowments are the log capital stock per worker and the Penn World Tables human capital index. Industry variables come from about 350 US six-digit NAICS manufacturing industries in 2012. An industry's dependence on institutions is asset intangibility (one minus the share of property, plant and equipment in assets) for financial institutions, the share of inputs that are neither traded on open exchanges nor reference priced (Rauch 1999) for judicial institutions, and the employment-weighted standard deviation of within-firm sales growth for labour market institutions. The clean index is minus one times the first principal component of two emission rates: the air pollution rate (itself the first principal component of log emissions per dollar of revenue for carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, PM2.5, sulphur dioxide and volatile organic compounds) and log water pollution emissions per dollar of revenue. All environmental variables are scaled so that higher values mean better environmental quality. Bilateral trade comes from BACI (134 countries plus a rest-of-world region), applied tariffs from Macmap, and Exiobase 3.8.1 (163 industries) supplies output and air emissions by country and industry for the decomposition and the quantitative model. Neither regression is causal, and the first does not separate comparative advantage from other channels. Countries with stronger financial and judicial institutions have significantly better air and water quality, while the relationship for labour market institutions is not significant. Across industries, the binned scatter plots (which put dependence on the vertical axis and the clean index on the horizontal axis) have slopes of 0.58 for financial, 0.49 for judicial and 0.18 for labour market institutions, with R-squared of 0.34, 0.24 and 0.03. The five cleanest manufacturing industries have a mean institutional dependence index of 0.65 and the five dirtiest a mean of , a gap of 2.12 standard deviations. Fluid power pumps (clean index 2.42) depend more than average on all three institutions, and gypsum products (clean index ) depend less on all three. The second line is the key assumption: productivity reflects the interaction of the exporter's institutional quality with the industry's institutional dependence , the interactions of factor endowments with factor intensities , the interaction of the stringency of environmental regulation with the clean index , and a stochastic term . Jakarta, a megacity of 32 million residents on a delta where thirteen rivers meet the sea, already suffers about 300 million dollars of flood damages per year. Global sea level rise combines with land subsidence of 7 to 14 cm per year, driven by groundwater extraction, and official plans describe 3 to 5 m of relative sea level rise by 2050. The government has responded with a proposed sea wall costing up to 60 billion dollars and with a new political capital, Nusantara. The core argument is a commitment problem in the spirit of Kydland and Prescott (1977): the government would prefer ex ante not to protect coastal development, but once development is sunk it is ex post optimal to protect it, so developers over-build at the coast and force defense. Reference : Hsiao, Moscona and Sastry (2026) Model Setting The paper asks whether governments systematically intervene in agricultural markets when climate extremes hit, why they do so, and what this implies for global adaptation to a warming world. The motivating case is India's wheat export ban of May 2022, announced after a heat wave cut output by about 10 percent: it protected Indian consumers, was attacked as "antifarmer" at home, and pushed world wheat prices up by 6 percent. The authors build a global panel of agricultural policy and extreme heat exposure by country, crop and year since 1980 and establish two facts with opposite signs. Extreme heat that hits domestic production leads to consumer-assisting policy that lowers domestic prices relative to world prices; extreme heat that hits foreign production leads to producer-assisting policy that raises them. A model in the tradition of Grossman and Helpman (1994), Goldberg and Maggi (1999) and Maggi and Rodriguez-Clare (2000), in which a government sets a border tax to maximize a weighted sum of consumer surplus, producer surplus and government revenue, rationalizes both facts: a sufficiently redistribution-focused government moves policy with the country's self-sufficiency, which domestic and foreign shocks push in opposite directions. Finally, an empirical equilibrium model built directly on the regression estimates quantifies who gains and who loses from the policy responses: domestic consumers are shielded, domestic producers and foreign consumers lose, and the global incidence is regressive. Reference : Duflo et al. (2018) Model Setting The paper asks whether regulatory discretion helps or hurts the enforcement of pollution standards. The setting is Gujarat, India, where the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) regulates about 20,000 industrial plants under strict emission limits. Penalties are severe when applied (in 2008 the GPCB ordered 9% of sample plants to close, at least temporarily, sometimes by cutting off water and electricity), but the chance of being caught is low: the regulator has a limited inspection budget and chooses which plants to inspect, so half of plants are inspected less often than the prescribed rate while similar plants are inspected many times more. Discretion would hurt if plants bribe to avoid inspections or the regulator shirks; it would help if the regulator uses local information to target the dirtiest plants. The paper combines a two-year field experiment on 960 plants with a structural model. The experimental treatment bundled two changes: more inspection resources, and the removal of discretion over the extra inspections, which were assigned at random. Because the treatment changes both at once, the model is needed to separate the value of resources from the value of discretion. The model has two stages. In the targeting stage , a benevolent regulator chooses an inspection rule, based on plant observables and a noisy signal of pollution, to maximize abatement subject to an inspection budget; plants decide whether to run their abatement equipment given the inspection threat. In the penalty stage , after an initial inspection, a regulatory machine follows fixed rules for followup and punishment, and plants solve a single-agent dynamic problem of when to comply. The penalty stage delivers the value to a plant of being inspected at a given pollution level, which drives abatement incentives in the targeting stage. The model abstracts from corruption in the assignment of inspections (bribes during inspections are allowed). Experimental Design and Data From a population of 3455 red-category (high pollution potential) small and medium plants in Ahmedabad, Surat and Valsad, the authors drew 960 plants: all 473 audit-eligible plants in Ahmedabad and Surat and 488 randomly chosen audit-ineligible plants. Between August 2009 and May 2011, the 481 treatment plants were assigned at least one annual initial inspection and up to four per year: one in the first quarter, then a new inspection each quarter with probability 0.66. Each morning inspection teams received a random list of treatment plants. Treatment and control inspection reports entered the same database without a flag, were analyzed by the same labs, and were followed up by the same officials. The regulator kept discretion over its existing inspection budget in both arms. Data come from an independent end-line survey (April to July 2011) of pollution and abatement costs, and from 9624 GPCB documents that the authors code into actions of the regulator (inspect, warn, punish, accept) and the plant (comply, ignore), linked into chains of interactions. In these chains 87% end after a single inspection, with the regulator accepting in the third round. Experimental Evidence The treatment was implemented: control plants were inspected 1.40 times per year, and treatment plants an additional 1.71 times (3.11 in total), with initial inspections up by 1.50 per year. Treatment plants were 0.21 more likely to have a pollution reading collected (control base 0.38), 0.22 more likely to be found above a standard, and received more citations (0.20) and closure warnings (0.077). But costly penalties (closure directions, equipment mandates, utility disconnections) did not rise significantly. The treatment reduced end-line pollution by 0.105 standard deviations (standard error 0.084), insignificant, and raised compliance by 3.7 percentage points (standard error 2.1) on a base of 61%, with mass shifting from just above to just below the standard. Maintenance spending rose by 838 dollars (standard error 499). Three facts point to status quo targeting . First, the treatment cut the share of plants inspected below the prescribed rate from 50% to 13% but did not raise the number of plants with five or more inspections. Second, it did not find more extreme violators: 35 (10) treatment plants had a reading above five (ten) times the standard against 33 (12) in the control. Third, control-group end-line readings, which the regulator never saw, predict future inspections conditional on observables and past readings, so the regulator has its own pollution signals. Random inspections mostly found modest violators whom the regulator would not have punished anyway.
