Reference : Blundell, Gowrisankaran and Langer (2020) Model Setting The paper quantifies the value of dynamic enforcement , in which regulatory actions depend on a plant's history of past violations and investments, in the enforcement of the US Clean Air Act Amendments (CAAA). The EPA designates repeat or egregious offenders as high priority violators (HPV) and subjects them to more inspections and higher fines. Such escalation mechanisms increase marginal deterrence for repeat violations while avoiding over-fining plants before they have a chance to fix one-time violations, which is valuable when fines are costly to the regulator, when remediation is slow and stochastic, when inspections give imperfect information, and when the regulator cannot contract on heterogeneous plant costs. The authors build a discrete-time dynamic game between a plant and a regulator. The regulator's inspection, violation, fine and status-transition behavior is captured by estimated conditional choice probabilities (CCPs) rather than by an estimated regulator utility function, and plants choose when to invest in pollution abatement. The plant cost parameters are allowed to differ across plants through a nonparametric random coefficients distribution on a fixed grid, estimated by a convex GMM estimator in the spirit of Fox et al. (2011) and Nevo, Turner and Williams (2016). The data are a quarterly panel from EPA's ECHO enforcement database, 2007:I-2013:III, with 2,355,908 plant/quarter observations on 107,705 plants in the seven most polluting NAICS sectors, merged with NEI emissions, AP3 county marginal damages and NAAQS non-attainment status. Counterfactuals that change the state-contingent fine policy show that removing dynamic enforcement would raise pollution damages by 164 percent holding fines constant, or raise fines by 519 percent holding damages constant. Enforcement Institutions and Data Facts Enforcement is carried out largely by ten EPA regions and by state agencies, so regions and states differ in budgets and enforcement preferences. All plants are inspected regularly; an inspection or a self-report may uncover a violation, moving the plant into regular violator status, where it faces more inspections and possible fines, and it returns to compliance only once all violations are resolved. Fines combine a gravity component (actual or potential harm, toxicity, sensitivity of the receiving environment, duration, history of noncompliance, ability to pay) and the economic benefit of noncompliance; political pressure, bankruptcy laws and caps limit the EPA's ability to levy large penalties. HPV status, assigned through ten general and five matrix criteria (some explicitly dynamic, such as "chronic or recalcitrant violator"), triggers intense oversight, higher fines and deadlines, and can be exited only after all violations are resolved. Compliance is high: 95.6 percent of plant/quarters are in compliance and 88.4 percent of plants are never out of compliance, while only 4.2 percent ever enter HPV status. Investment, inferred from ECHO resolution codes (94 percent of investments), PSD permits and HPV exits, occurs in 4.9 percent of regular-violator quarters and 17.5 percent of HPV quarters. Investment last quarter raises the probability of returning to compliance by 38 percentage points; an HPV plant that did not invest last quarter stays HPV with certainty, while one that did has a 49 percent chance of moving to compliance, 26 percent of moving to regular violator status and 25 percent of staying HPV. Investments made while in compliance raise subsequent violation rates, so they are treated as economic rather than prophylactic and are not counted. About 30 percent of investments are followed by another within six quarters, versus about 2.3 percent under i.i.d. investment, which motivates random coefficients. Reference : Kang and Silveira (2021) Model Setting The paper quantifies the benefits of regulatory discretion in the enforcement of water pollution rules in California. Penalties for observably similar violations differ across dischargers ( disparities in punishment ), and two stories can explain this: regulators may differ in their own preferences (how much they care about pollution, how costly it is for them to punish), or they may use their expertise to tailor penalties to dischargers whose compliance costs differ. The paper builds a principal-agent model in the spirit of Becker (1968) and Mookherjee and Png (1994) in which a regulator sets a penalty schedule for each facility, and the facility, privately informed about its compliance cost, chooses an unobserved negligence level that stochastically generates violations. The model is nonparametrically identified by combining the facility first-order condition with an exogenous increase in enforcement stringency in 2006 (following d'Haultfoeuille and Fevrier 2020) and the regulator first-order condition (following Luo, Perrigne and Vuong 2018). The estimates show that most of the heterogeneity in penalties comes from heterogeneity in compliance costs , not in regulator preferences , and that removing discretion (a one-size-fits-all schedule or a linear schedule) raises penalties and enforcement costs while increasing violations by facilities whose violations the regulator views as most harmful. Institutional Setting and Data Discharges into surface waters are regulated through NPDES permits under the Clean Water Act and California's Porter-Cologne Act. Permittees submit self-monitoring reports; 95% of recorded violations in 2000-2014 were self-reported. Enforcement is carried out by nine Regional Water Quality Control Boards (seven part-time members appointed by the governor, relying on technical staff), overseen by the State Water Resources Control Board. The enforcement policy gives a penalty methodology (initial amount based on extent, severity and sensitivity of the receiving water, then adjustments for conduct, ability to pay, economic benefit, enforcement costs and environmental justice) but leaves wide room for discretion; the board's final penalty differs from the staff assessment in 24% of actions. Serious violations (exceeding limits for a group I pollutant by 40% or a group II pollutant by 20%) and chronic nonserious violations (four or more in six months) are subject to a mandatory minimum penalty (MMP) of 3,000 dollars per violation. Enforcement resources differ a lot across boards (from 109 to 539 permits per enforcement staff member). The source of identifying variation is the 2006 institutional changes : the launch of the CIWQS electronic tracking and reporting system (July 2005) and the creation of a statewide Office of Enforcement (July 2006). Both lowered the administrative burden of enforcement. Reference : Chen et al. (2025) Model Setting The paper studies how incomplete regulation of large firms interacts with business groups (conglomerates) . The setting is China's Top 1,000 Energy Conservation Program, announced by the National Development and Reform Commission in April 2006 as part of the 11th Five-Year Plan (11FYP), whose national goal was to cut energy intensity by 20 percent between 2006 and 2011. The program covered the 1,008 industrial firms in nine energy-intensive industries whose 2004 energy consumption exceeded 180,000 tons of coal equivalent (tce); together they used 670 million tce in 2004, 47 percent of industrial and 33 percent of total Chinese energy use. Because selection was based on retrospective 2004 energy use and the list never changed, participation could not be manipulated. Although the stated goals were energy efficiency and a saving of 100 million tce by 2011, in practice local officials (whose promotion was tied to meeting provincial targets) enforced firm-level energy use quotas based on historical energy use and expected industry growth, checked by annual third-party audits. In 2012 the program was expanded into the Top 10,000 Energy Conservation and Carbon Reduction Program, covering 16,078 firms with 2010 energy use above 10,000 tce; Top 10,000 firms that were not in the Top 1,000 were unregulated during the 11FYP and serve as controls. Data combine firm energy use from the China Environmental Statistics Database (CESD, 2001-2010), output and characteristics from the Annual Survey of Industrial Firms (ASIF), tax survey data for robustness, and shareholder records from China's Administrative Registration Data (CARD), used to build ownership networks (wholly owned subsidiaries, partly owned firms, shareholders, and firms owned by the shareholders, with at least 25 percent ownership at each of up to two levels). Top 1,000 firms have 2,466 related firms in the same four-digit industry, 2.45 per regulated firm, and a related firm is on average 19.3 percent as large as its regulated counterpart. Within conglomerates size falls almost geometrically with rank: the second-largest firm is 29 percent as large as the largest, and conglomerates with larger leading firms have more firms. The paper proceeds in three steps: difference-in-differences (DiD) designs for the effects on regulated firms, on related firms, and on unrelated firms in more exposed industries; an industry equilibrium model of conglomerate production with Melitz (2003) monopolistic competition, in which the regulation is a quota on the energy use of the largest affiliate; and policy analysis that computes aggregate energy savings, the government willingness to pay that rationalizes the program, and alternative policies such as conglomerate-level regulation and energy taxes. Reference : Aronoff and Rafey (2026) Model Setting The paper builds an empirical framework for valuing environmental offset markets and applies it to Florida wetlands. Under the Clean Water Act and the 1972 Florida Water Resources Act, regulators enforce a No Net Loss rule: a landowner may develop a protected wetland only if the loss is offset by an equal gain elsewhere in the same hydrological region. Since the Florida banking rules of 1994, the offsets are produced by wetland mitigation banks , long-lived firms that place private land under a permanent conservation easement, restore or create wetlands, and receive certified offset credits from the regulator over time as restoration is verified. Developers buy credits bilaterally (often through brokers) from banks located in the same service area , a market boundary that approximates a hydrological region. The regulator converts wetland attributes into credits with a uniform assessment method that captures ecological and hydrological functions, but it does not account for the flood protection that wetlands provide to nearby property. The new data cover 1995-2018: an administrative ledger of all state offset transactions, contracts and release schedules for every bank, transaction prices from a private broker and public-records requests, 30-m NOAA C-CAP land cover maps for 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016, public land ownership, and FEMA flood insurance claims, policies and flood hazard maps, all matched to 1,378 local watersheds (1,004 inside offset markets). Five facts motivate the model. Cumulative sales were about 1.1 billion dollars (2020 dollars), growing about 9.8% per year. Markets are concentrated: fewer than three banks trade in an average market, the median bank produces about 200 credits over its life while the median developer buys 1.1 credits, and the average bank owns 26.1% of its market's production potential. Banks take time to build: the regulator typically releases 15% of a bank's credits every 3 years, about 18.2 years for a full project, and the median bank holds 52% of its credits in reserve. Prices (about 88,000 dollars per credit) exceed observed bank costs (about 24,000 dollars per credit). Finally, trade relocates wetlands from densely developed, flood-exposed cores to peripheral watersheds near public conservation land. The model has three blocks: (1) many small, myopic landowners decide each period whether to develop their wetland, which requires buying credits at the market price (offset demand); (2) a few large banks enter by paying a sunk cost, receive credits on a fixed release schedule, and sell them over time in a dynamic oligopoly with storage (offset supply); (3) flood damages in each watershed depend on wetlands lost to development and wetlands restored by banks. Gains from trade are measured relative to the pre-market benchmark of direct conservation , under which the wetlands that were developed would have been conserved and the banks would not have entered. A conservation contract is socially valuable only to the extent that it changes behavior, but landowners who would have conserved anyway tend to have low costs of accepting a contract and therefore win procurement mechanisms that screen on cost alone. The setting is the USDA's Conservation Reserve Program (CRP), one of the largest payments for ecosystem services (PES) schemes in the world, which pays landowners 1.6 to 1.8 billion dollars per year to retire cropland and undertake conservation actions under (typically ten-year) contracts. The key object is the demand for deforestation : how much private land farmers would keep in agriculture as the private value of forest relative to agriculture rises by dollars per hectare. The demand is identified from regional variation in transportation costs to ports, which shift farmgate prices. Rescaling transportation costs ($/ton) by local yields (tons/ha) converts them into $/ha, so a change in transport costs is equivalent to a land use tax or payment. Transportation costs are instrumented with straight-line distances to the nearest port and state capital, and heterogeneous responses are captured with instrumental variable quantile regression (IVQR). Reference : Harstad (2024) Model Setting The paper builds a deliberately simple dynamic game to show how international trade and the exploitation of a depletable natural resource interact, and how trade policy can be redesigned to reverse the negative interactions. The South ( ) owns a resource stock (the leading example is a tropical rainforest), and the North ( ) suffers a damage whenever the resource is exploited. Logging produces timber and converts forest into agricultural land (beef), and both products can be exported to . The motivating episode is the 2019 EU–Mercosur agreement, concluded while deforestation in the Amazon was rising, and the 2020 proposal by France and the Netherlands to link tariff reductions to the implementation of sustainability provisions. The paper delivers two sets of results. Under a standard free trade agreement (FTA), (1) trade causes exploitation , because export prices exceed domestic valuations; (2) exploitation causes trade , because an FTA is only socially valuable once little resource is left to lose; and (3) exploits in order to obtain trade, so the parties end up trading and depleting even when the damage exceeds the gains from trade. Four empirical patterns motivate the model (FAO data, 1990-2020): (1) global forest area fell by 7.1%, with about 90% of the loss in tropical countries and regrowth in Europe and China; (2) deforestation moves with agricultural land expansion; (3) countries with a revealed comparative advantage in agriculture in 1990 expanded agricultural land and lost more forest; (4) deforestation follows from a country's own population growth and that of its main trading partners. The model has a market for new land: a land-clearing sector uses labor to convert open-access forests into agricultural land, and forward-looking landowners buy new land and rent it to producers. Three mechanisms shape land use: (1) structural change determines the size of agriculture and the aggregate demand for land; (2) comparative advantage distributes the pressure on land across countries; (3) forward-looking land accumulation determines the timing of forest responses. Reference : Araujo, Costa and Sant'Anna (2026) Model Setting The paper estimates the carbon-efficient forest cover of the Brazilian Amazon, defined as the land use that would arise if farmers fully internalized the social cost of the carbon stored in each plot of forest. It builds a dynamic discrete choice model in which profit-maximizing agents choose every year whether each field is used for crops, pasture or forest, subject to conversion costs and with forward-looking option values. The model is estimated on a panel of land use for more than 5.7 billion 30-m pixels in each year 2008-2017 (MapBiomas), combined with potential yields (FAO GAEZ), crop prices at regional trade hubs (ESALQ), newly computed transportation costs to export ports, and a 30-m map of aboveground biomass (Zarin et al. 2016). The sample is pixels outside protected areas that were not deforested before 2000. Estimation follows Scott (2013): the CCP structure and one-period finite dependence deliver an Euler-type equation that is a linear regression with transition probabilities on the left-hand side, so the value function never has to be solved during estimation. The setting motivates three features. First, deforestation is driven by pasture: between 2008 and 2017, 90% of the deforested area became pasture for extensive cattle ranching, and 7% of 2008 forest became pasture by 2017 versus only 1% that became cropland. Second, deforestation is not a one-way street: 13% of 2008 pasture had reverted to forest by 2017, so the model allows regeneration. Third, both private returns (yields, transport costs) and social damages (carbon density) vary sharply over space, so the conservation trade-off is local and policies that ignore this heterogeneity are inefficient. The key counterfactuals compare the business-as-usual (BAU) steady state with the efficient one under a social cost of carbon of 50 US dollars per ton of CO , and evaluate a carbon tax (equivalently, a carbon-based payment for ecosystem services) and excise taxes on cattle and crops. Reference : Assunção et al. (2026) Model Setting The paper builds a spatial and dynamic model of efficient land allocation in the Brazilian Amazon biome. Each piece of land can be used for cattle ranching (about 85% of deforested, non-abandoned land is pasture, so agriculture is identified with cattle) or kept as forest. Deforestation releases the carbon stored in primary forest, while abandoned pasture regrows as secondary forest and slowly absorbs carbon. A fictitious social planner, who internalizes the emissions externality, trades off cattle revenue against the value of carbon at an exogenous emissions price. The paper does not model decentralized landowners: since monitoring and enforcement cut deforestation by more than 80% between 2004 and 2012, current deforestation is read as reflecting government valuations, and edge effects and fires make conservation a decision at a scale far above private holdings. Three ingredients distinguish the analysis from static or discrete-choice models of deforestation (e.g. Souza-Rodrigues (2019), Araujo, Costa and Sant'Anna (2025)): (1) explicit carbon accumulation dynamics in regrowing forests, so that reforestation , not only avoided deforestation, is a choice and transition paths over 15 to 30 years can be computed; (2) large cross-sectional heterogeneity in cattle productivity and carbon density, measured from census and satellite data on 1,043 sites (about 67.5 km by 67.5 km) or 78 coarse sites (about 270 km by 270 km); (3) uncertainty on two fronts: stochastic cattle prices following a Markov chain, and uncertain site productivities, handled with ambiguity aversion toward a baseline Bayesian posterior. The paper first infers a “business-as-usual” shadow price of emissions that rationalizes 1995–2008 deforestation, and then studies how international transfers of dollars per net ton of CO e captured change land use, carbon and Brazil's welfare. Reference : Salazar Restrepo and Leite Mariante (2026) Model Setting The paper asks whether spatially targeted forest conservation survives in general equilibrium, or whether the deforestation it prevents simply relocates, a phenomenon called leakage . It studies two flagship Brazilian policies over 2003-2018: the Priority List (from 2008), which singled out the municipalities with the highest deforestation rates for intensified command-and-control enforcement (embargoes, monitoring priority, credit and registration conditions), and the continuous creation of Protected Areas (Conservation Units and Indigenous Territories), where clearing is banned and which typically cover high-forest, low-deforestation regions. Reduced-form evidence shows both bind locally: a synthetic difference-in-differences design finds that listing cut total natural-vegetation loss by 0.44 log points (36%) while pasture area fell, cropland rose, agricultural value added per hectare rose by roughly 15% and cattle per hectare of pasture by roughly 20%; a spatial regression discontinuity finds forest cover 13-15 percentage points higher just inside Protected Areas. Such designs cannot measure leakage, because they assume untreated regions are unaffected. The authors build an open-economy quantitative spatial model of Brazil in which deforestation is an economic sector : clearing forest is a costly, decreasing-returns activity that endogenously supplies agricultural land, so each region has an upward-sloping supply curve of new land whose position reflects its deforestation productivity . The economy has 557 micro-regions indexed by (with for origin and destination) plus a rest of the world (RoW), agricultural goods (temporary crops, permanent crops, pasture-based cattle) produced with land and labor, and one non-agricultural good. Preferences are non-homothetic (PIGL), workers migrate across regions and select into sectors, goods are traded with iceberg costs, and land accumulates over time. Brazil is modeled as a sequence of static spatial equilibria linked by laws of motion for land and labor. The central theoretical message is that leakage depends on whether targeted deforestation is supply-driven (land is cheap to clear) or demand-driven (land is valuable once cleared), and Brazilian deforestation is predominantly supply-driven. Reference : Jia, Ma and Xie (2026) Model Setting The paper asks how flood risk , as opposed to realized flood events , shapes where firms locate and how much people work, and what this implies for aggregate output. Using county-level and zip-code-level US data for 1998-2018, the authors document two facts: (i) a rise in flood risk has a large, negative long-run effect on firm entry, employment and output; (ii) realized floods reduce output in the year they occur but have little effect on firm entry or employment. Flood risk is measured from digitized FEMA maps: the historic Q3 Flood Insurance Rate Maps for 1998 and the National Flood Hazard Layer for 2018. The measure is the share of a county's (or zip code's) land inside Special Flood Hazard Zones, which are areas with at least a 1 percent annual chance of inundation. On average this share rose by 6 percentage points between 1998 and 2018, and by 19 percentage points at the ninetieth percentile of county changes. Flood events come from the Dartmouth Flood Observatory (DFO). Firm entry, exit and employment come from the Census Business Dynamics Statistics, prime-age population from the Census, county real GDP from the BEA, and zip-code outcomes from the Zip Codes Business Patterns. The facts motivate a quantitative spatial model with Krugman (1980) free entry and McFadden (1978) location choice. Firms and workers make long-run decisions before floods are realized and anticipate flood risk; realized floods lower productivity and amenities and destroy some firms. In the calibrated model, flood risk lowered US aggregate output by 0.53 percent in 2018. Direct damages account for 23 percent of this loss and long-run adjustment by firms and workers for 77 percent. Brownian motion, also known as Brownian movement, is the random motion of particles suspended in a fluid (liquid or gas) resulting from their collision with the fast-moving atoms or molecules in the gas or liquid. This phenomenon is named after the Scottish botanist Robert Brown, who first observed it in 1827 while studying pollen particles floating in water under a microscope. Key Characteristics of Brownian Motion Randomness: The motion is erratic and unpredictable, with particles moving in random directions. Continuous Paths: Particles exhibit continuous but non-differentiable paths. Scale Independence: The motion occurs at microscopic scales and is independent of the size of the particles (as long as they are small enough). Dependence on Temperature: The intensity of Brownian motion increases with temperature, as higher temperatures result in faster-moving fluid molecules. Mathematical Description Brownian motion is mathematically described by the Wiener process, a continuous-time stochastic process. Key properties include: Mean Zero: The expected value of the displacement is zero. Variance Proportional to Time: The variance of the displacement increases linearly with time. Independent Increments: Displacements over non-overlapping time intervals are independent. Independent Increments: For any , the increments , ,..., are independent.
